title: COMPLEXITY AS A FEATURE OF INTERIOR DESIGN AND PLACE ATTACHMENT

findings.antecedent: Visual complexity of interior design (complex pictures with design elements)
findings.consequent: Preference to spend leisure time in a place
findings.source: 4.1.2. Preference To Spend Time In Front Of Design Elements, p. 72-73
findings.quote: participants rated complex pictures higher (M=3.66, SD= 1.863) compared to plain pictures (M=2.11, SD= 1.326). A paired-sample t-test revealed that the difference was significant (t (835) = 20.13, p<.001).

findings.antecedent: Visual complexity of interior design (complex pictures with design elements)
findings.consequent: Reaction time (time taken to rate pictures)
findings.quote: Participants took more time (in terms of milliseconds) while rating complex pictures (M= 7892.78, SD= 11466.435) in comparison with the time it took to rate plain pictures (M= 5863.34, SD=7401.660). The result of paired sample t-test revealed that the difference in reaction time was significant (t (835) = 4.31, p<.001).

limitations: The use of digital stimuli (cyber domain) and isolation of visual perception may lack ecological validity, potentially diverting from holistic sensory experiences.
The correlation between preference and openness to experience was only significant for non-reverse coded Turkish items, possibly due to their higher number in the inventory.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the effect of visual complexity in interior design on place attachment, measured by preference ratings and reaction times, and explored its relationship with individual differences in openness to experience and inclusion of nature to self. Key findings indicate that participants preferred complex interior designs over plain ones and spent more time looking at complex images. A positive correlation was found between openness to experience and preference for complex pictures, and also between inclusion of nature to self and openness to experience. A limitation noted was the potential lack of ecological validity due to the use of digital stimuli and the isolation of visual perception, as well as a specific statistical artifact related to the Big Five inventory items.
